text: January twenty-seventh, 1967. During a launch rehearsal, a spark inside Apollo 1 meets a cabin filled with pure oxygen.
Within seconds, fire races through the cabin. Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee are lost.
Fire in a spacecraft is not like fire on Earth. Without gravity, hot gas doesn't rise. A candle flame doesn't flicker upward. It becomes a dim, blue sphere.

We are Team Guatians, from Karachi. For NASA Space Apps 2026 we took on the challenge Flame in Freefall: turn decades of NASA's microgravity fire research into fire-safety insight for the Moon and Mars.

Here is why it matters now. So that astronauts can step into their spacesuits faster, lunar habitats and pressurized rovers will run on enriched air: at least thirty percent oxygen, at ten point two psi or less.
More oxygen means materials ignite more easily and burn harder. So the question is simple. Has anyone tested the materials we will bring, in the air we will breathe?
The answer is buried in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics database: hundreds of experiments, spread across more than twenty spreadsheets, each in its own format.
So we built Fire Atlas. A Python pipeline pulled every combustion investigation from NASA's open API. Twenty-five investigations. Twenty-two experiment tables.
We unified them into one thousand seven hundred and nineteen tests, converting atmospheres, bars and millimetres of mercury onto one scale, and keeping track of every value's source row.
Where NASA didn't record a value, we say so. Assumed values are flagged, drawn hollow, and never counted as evidence.

Then we put every test on one map. Oxygen runs left to right. Pressure runs bottom to top. Each point is a real experiment, colored by what happened: it burned, it went out on its own, or it never ignited.

The violet box is the planned lunar habitat. The curves show constant oxygen partial pressure. Notice that the Moon base sits almost on Earth's line, yet breathes sixty-three percent more oxygen by fraction.
Now switch on the solid materials: the fabrics and plastics that actually burn in a cabin.
All two hundred and sixty-three of them sit here, at Earth-like air. The highest oxygen level any solid was ever tested at is twenty-two point two percent.
Inside the lunar envelope? Zero solid tests. In three dimensions, the gap is even harder to miss.
Fire Atlas also answers questions. Ask it, in plain English: would acrylic panels burn in a lunar rover?
Our SI turns the question into cabin conditions, then writes a short briefing: what the data shows, what is missing, and which tests should be run next.

But we never let the SI do the math. Deterministic code computes ninety-seven facts first. The SI may only explain them, and a verifier removes any citation that doesn't exist and any number that isn't in the data.
Every sentence carries a receipt. Click one, and you see NASA's original spreadsheet row, unmodified, down to the typo in the column name.

Partial gravity has never been tested in this database. But SAFFIRE two tested the same materials at one g and in orbit. Silicone burned in three of four samples at one g, and in none of four in microgravity. The Moon sits between those bounds.
The readiness matrix makes it plain: six cabin materials have microgravity burn data, and not one has been tested at lunar oxygen levels.
Every investigation can be compared side by side, and every filtered test exports with its DOI, ready for flammability models.
Because this is safety data, we built Fire Atlas to be trustworthy, not just beautiful.

API keys never reach the browser; they live only on the server. Every input is validated and rate limited, and we tested prompt injection attacks. The SI ignores instructions hidden inside a question.

If every SI provider fails, the app falls back to a computed, fully cited briefing. And we state our limits openly: no partial-gravity data yet, unrecorded pressures are assumed, and these briefings support decisions. They do not certify materials.
The impact is direct. Fire Atlas shows mission planners which experiments to fly next, on missions like LUCI and FM2, before crews ever breathe lunar air.
And it matters on Earth too. Hospital rooms with oxygen-enriched air face the same question every day.
Fire Atlas. Every NASA fire test, on one map, with receipts. Find the gap before the fire does.
